title: Vayishlach: too small (Genesis 32:11)
hookLine: Jacob prays "I am not worthy of all the mercies"
carry: too small for all this kindness

cards: You're about to see someone you wronged a long time ago. A sibling, an ex, an old friend. You've rehearsed it in the shower a hundred times.

Then you hear they're coming, and they're bringing a crowd. This week's portion is called Vayishlach, and he sent. Jacob sends messengers ahead to his brother Esau, twenty years after he took his blessing.
They come back with news: Esau is coming to meet you, and four hundred men are with him.

teach.b: The Torah says Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed. Two words, and Rashi says they mean two different fears: afraid he'd be killed, and distressed that he might have to kill.
He splits his people into two camps, so that if one is attacked, the other can escape. Then he prays, and it's worth hearing how it goes.

teach.h: GOD OF MY FATHERS, YOU PROMISED.
teach.b: He begins with God's names: God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac. He reminds God of the promise: you told me, go home, and I'll do you good.
And then, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I am not worthy of all the mercies" and all the faithfulness you've shown your servant.
In Hebrew it's one word: katonti. I am small. I've become too small for all of this.
With only my staff I crossed this Jordan, he says, and now I've become two camps. Think about who's saying this: Jacob, rich now, with a big family, a man who's worked his way through twenty years.
His first move in danger isn't to list what he deserves. It's to say: I'm small, and I've been given so much. Only after that does he ask.
Save me, please, from my brother's hand, because I'm afraid of him.

teach.h: I AM NOT WORTHY OF ALL THE MERCIES.
teach.b: Plain fear, said out loud. Some teachers hold up this prayer as a model: gratitude first, honesty about being small, and then a direct request. Being small, here, isn't shame.
It's what makes the kindness visible.

how: Some teachers compare the shape of Jacob's prayer, praise and thanks first and then a request, to the Amidah, the central Jewish prayer, which opens by naming the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

o: and he sent, messengers sent ahead
and he divided, splitting into two camps
and he feared, Jacob's dread of Esau

games.q: what's inside the prayer — tap the pairs.

s: Jacob's prayer opens by listing what he deserves
he says he's too small, not worthy of all the mercies, before he asks.
Rashi reads afraid and distressed as two different fears
afraid he'd be killed; distressed that he might have to kill.
Jacob hid his fear in the prayer
he says it plainly: save me from my brother, because I'm afraid of him.

games.q: your brother is coming with four hundred men. you're Jacob. you pray. how do you begin?
o: say you're too small for all the kindness you've had.
ask right away to be saved.
games.why: Jacob begins with God's promise and his own smallness: I am not worthy of all the mercies. only then does he ask for help.

practice: Think of what you have that you once didn't, people, a roof, a skill, another morning, and let yourself feel small next to it, the good kind of small. Then name, plainly, the thing you're afraid of right now.
If you pray, you can use Jacob's words, I am not worthy of all the mercies, and then ask for help; if you don't, just hold both, the gifts and the fear.

wordCard.voice: Vayishlach. And he sent: the portion where Jacob, afraid of meeting his brother, prays that he's too small for all the kindness he's been shown.

orig.note: Hebrew: I am small. Jacob's word for being unworthy of all God's kindness.

carryVoice: Your line: too small for all this kindness. Thanks first, then the ask. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: I am not worthy of all the mercies
